title: Extremal laws for coupon collection with group drawings
description:
Unrefereed research candidate. A collector wants a full set of n different coupons (stickers, cards, DNA fragments), but each box holds a group of s of them at once. Whoever fills the boxes decides how the groups overlap. How quickly can a full set be completed, and how slowly can it be made while staying fair, meaning every coupon is equally common?

What was known. Grunbaum and Yaakobi conjectured that drawing uniformly from all possible groups (the full model) is the slowest fair rule. Barak-Pelleg and Berend disproved this with the seven-point Fano plane and asked how slow a fair rule can be and how large the excess over the full model can become. On the fast side, Fang and Chang (2014) solved the case where boxes hold half the coupons and conjectured that equal disjoint groups are fastest whenever s divides n.

Results. (1) When the omitted coupons can form a Steiner 2-design, sampling it is the slowest fair rule after every number of draws, and this characterises the design (seven coupons in boxes of four: mean 47/12 against 257/68 for the full model). (2) In every critical window where a draw omits a fraction p of n coupons and npk → λ, the slowest fair mean is k + min(1, λ) + o(1), against k + 1 − e−λ for the full model; Barak-Pelleg and Berend's star mechanism already reaches k + 1 in its own windows (λ > 1), and the new parts are the matching upper bound, every λ, every n and the peak excess 1/e. (3) For every n and omitted size r, no fair rule is more than 1/e + (1 − γ)/ln(n/r) draws slower on average than the full model; this is below one draw when boxes hold at least half the coupons, and the limit 1/e is attained. (4) An exhaustive exact search of all fair mechanisms for n ≤ 7 (and n = 8 with s = 2 or 6), up to 2,505,121 families, shows that the Fano plane attains the maximum at Barak-Pelleg and Berend's own seven-coupon example and that six coupons in boxes of three is the smallest case where the full model is not slowest. (5) For any law on boxes of size at most s, the mean is at least max{xHx, 1 + x} with x = n/s: equal disjoint groups are uniquely fastest when s divides n, which proves the Fang–Chang conjecture, and complementary partitions are uniquely fastest when n − s divides n. The h = 1 product bound is Pelekis–Ramon–Wang's Theorem 2.6 after Poissonisation (Finner's generalized Hölder inequality); Berend and Sher introduced the complementary-decomposition law and computed its mean.

Limits. The critical-window result is asymptotic and converges slowly (at n = 1600 the full model is still 0.03 draws above its limit), and its construction is existential. The exact slowest rule without a design is known only for small n; whether the excess can grow without bound for small boxes is open; the fastest rule is open when neither s nor n − s divides n.

Contents. The paper (LaTeX source and PDF), the figure, an exact-arithmetic verification script, a C enumeration of all small fair mechanisms with an exact-rational certificate, the figure script and the recorded outputs, plus the bibliography, a machine-readable index, a research-gate record, a review summary, a replay receipt and SHA-256 sums. Every check exits with an error on failure, also under python -O.

Assurance. Written proofs; the computations test the stated finite cases. Internal AI-assisted review only: a combined five-role Claude review panel, one revision round, a re-review, a proof audit of the new proofs and a clean replay with negative controls. No Astra/Codex review took place. This is not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Text CC0-1.0; code MIT.
